title: The Vote
setting: a beekeeper moving hives by night

post.author: u/night_hives_ragnfrid
post.title: I move bees at night. At 3 AM my booked orchard row was full of someone else's hives, and our booking system says I never booked. I have the email.

blocks.text: I keep bees and move them at night, when every bee is home and the hive shut. It's spring here: growers rent our hives for their blossom, and our cooperative books each load into an orchard row of 40 hives.
Bookings live on three computers that answer over the internet, called servers: A in our extraction shed, B and C in the office. Each keeps the same record: a numbered list of bookings.

One server, the leader, takes every booking in three steps: add it to the end of its record as a numbered line, an entry; have Hivebook, our booking app, email the member a confirmation; then copy the entry to the other two. Valley-floor phones book through A; hill-farm phones through B or C, which pass bookings on.
If B and C hear nothing from the leader for 30 seconds, a wait called the election timeout, they hold an election: each says its record's length; the longest leads, a tie goes to B.

A split is when servers can't reach each other. When they meet again, at a rejoin, the same rule picks one leader and copies its record over the others. Hedvig, our secretary, wrote it four seasons ago.
Each entry also carries a timestamp: the time on its server's clock when it was stored.

On Thursday 22 October at 00:45 the frost warning lifted, so the growers opened their rows for the night, first come, first served; blossom was due at first light. Seventy of us booked in forty minutes; most nights see five. At 01:12 I booked row 7 of the river-road apple orchard. Hivebook emailed: "Booking 112 confirmed."
At 03:00 I pulled in. Row 7 was full: forty hives humming under my headlamp, none mine. Hivebook found no booking in my name; booking 112 is someone else's, made at 00:58 for another orchard.
I have the email. The record says I never booked.
I phoned Hedvig. She sent the servers' log, their diary of events. Each line: time, server, event, entries in its record.

00:50:00  A  link to B and C lost                 100
00:50:30  B  election: tie at 100, B leads         100
01:12:40  B  #112 row 7, on B and C, confirmed     112
01:18:48  A  #137 row 7 (Tormod), confirmed        137
01:30:00  A  rejoin: A 150, B 120; A leads         150
01:30:00  B  101 to 120 replaced by A's copy       150

On Wednesday a contractor fitted a new network switch in the shed: the box joining A's cable to the office. It failed at 00:50 and restarted itself at 01:30. A has its own internet line, so the valley floor still reached it.
A never knew it was cut off. It kept leading, storing and confirming 50 bookings; its copies went nowhere. B and C elected B and took the hills' 20, mine among them, each stored on both.

At 01:30 the longest record won: A's copy replaced entries 101 to 120. Tormod booked row 7 on A at 01:18; two confirmed bookings for one row is what Hedvig calls a conflict. Before Wednesday's switch, A had never been cut off while taking bookings.

blocks.label: switch_night.png

diagram.aria: The night of Thursday 22 October, from 00:45 to 01:32. Row one, the shed switch: working until 00:50, failed for 40 minutes, working again from 01:30. Row two, server A: leading alone and confirming bookings from 00:50 to 01:30. Row three, servers B and C: working throughout, overwritten at 01:30. Markers: the cut at 00:50:00, B elected at 00:50:30, booking 112 for row 7 confirmed on B and C at 01:12:40, booking 137 for row 7 confirmed by A alone at 01:18:48, and the longest record winning at 01:30:00.

blocks.caption: Redrawn from Hedvig's log, Thursday 22 October 2026. Red on A's row is A leading alone while the switch was down: it stored and confirmed 50 bookings that never reached B or C. B and C elected B at 00:50:30 and stored 20 bookings on both, mine at 01:12:40. At 01:30 A held 150 entries and B 120, both sharing the first 100, so A's copy was written over B and C.

blocks.text: My hives waited on the headland. Hedvig swaps the switch on Saturday; the pear rows open next week. Twenty of us were told "confirmed", then erased. What should we change?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: More than half of your servers, two of the three, is called a majority. Before you choose, read the log again. When A confirmed Tormod's booking, how many servers held it? When B confirmed yours, how many? At 01:30, was either record up to date, meaning it held every booking a member had been told was confirmed? And what does a record's length tell you about that?

replies.author: u/night_hives_ragnfrid
replies.text: Tormod's: A alone, one of three. Mine: B and C, two of three. At 01:30 neither record held everything: A lacked our 20, B and C lacked A's 50. Length only says A took more bookings.

comments.author: u/most_work_wins_godfrey
comments.text: The longest record has the most work in it, so it should win; that's just common sense. A took 50 bookings, B took 20: the rule saved 50 and cost 20. The real fault is B and C calling an election after 30 seconds of quiet. Lengthen the election timeout so a short cut never starts one, and there's only ever one leader.

replies.author: u/night_hives_ragnfrid
replies.text: Hedvig likes this one. One setting, nothing new to run.

comments.author: u/latest_stamp_mordecai
comments.text: Copying a whole record over another is the bug. Go booking by booking: where two bookings hold one row, keep the one with the newer timestamp, the more recent decision. Everything else from both sides stays.

reply.prompt: The pear rows open next week, and the bookings will rush again. What should the cooperative change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: After a split, let the server whose booking has the newest timestamp win each conflict.
options.part2: On Monday 26 October Hedvig changed the rejoin rule: the two records are merged booking by booking, and where two bookings hold one row, the newer timestamp stays. In the sim, replaying 22 October: three rows were booked on both sides that night. The hills' 103 (00:54:40) lost to A's 108 (00:55:36); A's 141 (01:22:00) lost to the hills' 117 (01:22:40); and mine, stamped 01:12:40, lost to Tormod's 01:18:48. Three confirmed bookings erased instead of twenty, and mine still among them. The stamps came from two servers' clocks that nobody had ever compared.
options.senior: Newest timestamp wins is last writer wins, and it leans on Rule 6's warning: never trust the clock on the wall. Two servers' clocks never agree exactly, so the newer stamp may be the earlier booking. Worse, it still erases bookings that were confirmed: once both sides of a split have told a member yes, any merge rule must take one yes back. The fix has to stop the second yes: confirm only what a majority holds, so two sides of a split can never both confirm.

options.text: Confirm a booking only once a majority stores it, and elect only up-to-date servers.
options.part2: On Monday 26 October Hedvig moved the bookings onto etcd, a small program that keeps one record on three servers by a set of voting rules called Raft. A booking is now confirmed only once two of the three have stored it, every election starts a new numbered term, and a server votes only for a candidate whose record is at least as up to date as its own. In the sim, replaying 22 October: A stores its 50 valley bookings and confirms none; those apps show waiting. At 00:50:30 B starts term 2, C votes for it, and B confirms 20, mine at 01:12:40. At 01:30 B's message carries term 2, A steps down, and its 50 unconfirmed entries are replaced; the valley sends them again. Confirmed bookings erased: 0. Row 7 stays mine. On the pear night the new switch held.
options.senior: Confirm only what a majority has stored, and two sides of a split can never both confirm: any two majorities of three share a server. Elect only a candidate whose record is at least as up to date, comparing the last entry's term first and then length, and every confirmed booking survives a change of leader, because the voters that elect a leader always include a server that holds it. Terms let a stale leader learn it is stale and step down. That is Raft; take it from etcd or ZooKeeper rather than writing your own. The price is honest: the side cut off from the majority can confirm nothing until it rejoins.

options.text: Confirm a booking only after all three servers have stored it, so none can ever be lost.
options.verdict: Trade-off: one slow server stops all
options.part2: On Monday 26 October Hedvig changed Hivebook: a booking is confirmed only when A, B and C have all stored it. In the sim, replaying 22 October: from 00:50 to 01:30 no booking could be confirmed anywhere, 40 minutes with seventy of us trying. At 01:30 A's longer record still won, A's 50 were confirmed, and our 20 waiting bookings were dropped and sent again. Nothing confirmed was lost. Then Hedvig replayed the night with no cut but C slow, storing one entry every 2 minutes: every booking waited for C, mine was confirmed at 02:10:00 and the last at 03:04:00, after I should have been at the orchard.
options.senior: Waiting for every copy does mean nothing confirmed is ever lost, and some systems accept that for small, rare writes. But it ties every booking to the slowest and least reachable server: one server down, slow or cut off stops bookings for everyone, so three servers become less available than one. A majority gives the same safety for confirmed bookings and keeps working with one server out.

options.text: Lengthen the election timeout so a brief cut never makes B and C start an election.
options.verdict: A later election, the same loss
options.part2: On Monday 26 October Hedvig set the election timeout to 10 minutes. In the sim, replaying 22 October: B and C waited until 01:00:00 to elect B, and five hill bookings sat waiting until then. A, which never knew it was cut off, confirmed its 50 alone all the same. At 01:30 A's 150 entries beat B's 120, and the same 20 confirmed bookings were erased, mine among them. The longer wait only gave the hills ten minutes with no leader.
options.senior: The election timeout decides how fast a new leader is chosen, not whether the old one may still confirm. A cut-off leader that confirms on its own copy does so for as long as the cut lasts, and any timeout shorter than the cut still gives you two leaders. A timeout longer than every cut means waiting that long whenever the leader really dies. Safety must come from the confirming rule, a majority, and the voting rule, up-to-date candidates only; then the timeout can be tuned for speed.

sim.title: Replay the 40 minutes the shed switch was down
sim.lede: You're Ragnfrid on Thursday 22 October 2026 at 00:40:00, before the cut. As given data: servers A (extraction shed), B and C (office) each hold the same 100 entries, and A leads. The shed switch fails at 00:50:00 and restarts at 01:30:00. The valley floor sends 50 bookings to A, one every 48 seconds from 00:50:00; the hill farms send 20 to B or C, one every 2 minutes from 00:50:40. Yours is the hills' twelfth: 01:12:40, entry 112, row 7. Three rows are booked on both sides: A's 108 (00:55:36) with the hills' 103 (00:54:40), Tormod's 137 (01:18:48) with your 112 for row 7, and A's 141 (01:22:00) with the hills' 117 (01:22:40). A slow C stores one entry every 2 minutes. Set when a booking counts as confirmed, what happens when A rejoins, the cut, the election timeout and a slow C, then play 00:40 to 01:31.
sim.tryThis: Try this: play it as built: A 150 entries against B's 120, 20 confirmed bookings erased, yours among them. Newest timestamp at rejoin: 3 erased, yours still one. Election timeout 10 minutes: B leads from 01:00:00, still 20. All three: 40 minutes with no booking confirmed, 0 erased. A majority with raft: A confirms none of its 50, B confirms 20 in term 2, 0 erased. A majority with longest wins: 20 erased again. Raft with confirm after one: 50 erased. No cut, all three, slow C: the last booking confirmed at 03:04:00.

explain.oneLine: Nothing broke the record; its rules did. A, cut off, kept confirming bookings on its own copy, B and C confirmed others, and at the rejoin the longest record won and erased 20 confirmed bookings. Confirm only what a majority has stored, and elect only a server whose record is up to date: that is Raft.

steps.title: Why longest wins erased confirmed bookings.
steps.text: A confirmed each booking once it alone had stored it: one copy of three. B confirmed each of the hills' bookings on two copies of three. At the rejoin the rule went in two steps: compare lengths, then copy the longer record over the others. Length counts how many bookings a server took, not which of them were promised to members, so A's 150 entries beat B's 120 and the 20 bookings stored on two servers were written over. What went wrong at each step: confirming on one copy let both sides of the split say yes, and the length rule then chose which yes to break.

steps.title: Raft, step by step: copying an entry.
steps.text: In Raft the record is called the log. First, the leader adds the booking to its log, marked with the number of its current leadership, called the term. Second, it sends the entry to the other servers, the followers. Third, each follower saves it and answers. Fourth, once a majority holds it, two of three here, the entry is committed, and only then is the member told it is confirmed. What can go wrong: a leader cut off from the majority, like A, can add entries but never commit them, so it never confirms one. A swarm of bees choosing a new home works the same way: it moves only once enough scouts agree on one site.

steps.title: Elections, terms and the vote that says no.
steps.text: A follower that hears nothing from a leader for its election timeout becomes a candidate. In steps: it adds one to the term, votes for itself and asks the others. Each server votes at most once per term, and only for a candidate whose log is at least as up to date as its own: the last entry's term is compared first, then the length. A candidate with votes from a majority leads. A leader or candidate that sees a higher term steps down. What can go wrong: two candidates split the vote; each waits a random time and tries again in a new term. The up-to-date rule is what protects confirmed entries: any majority that elects must include a server holding every committed entry, and it refuses a candidate that lacks them.

steps.title: Paxos, etcd and ZooKeeper.
steps.text: Paxos, from Leslie Lamport, is the older family that solved the same problem first: a value is chosen once a majority of servers accept the same numbered proposal, and any later proposal must carry that value forward. It is proven safe and famously hard to follow, which is why Raft was designed to be easier to teach. You rarely write either. etcd keeps a small record on several servers, usually three or five, with Raft, and Kubernetes keeps its cluster state there; ZooKeeper is the other common choice. Raft's log is Rule 1 for a group: write it in the logbook before you do it, so each server saves an entry before it answers.

steps.title: Why the other fixes fail.
steps.text: Newest timestamp wins merges the records but still erases confirmed bookings, and it trusts two servers' clocks (Rule 6). A longer election timeout only delays B's election; A confirms alone all the same. Confirming on all three loses nothing confirmed, but one slow or cut-off server stops every booking. Nightly backups don't help either: a copy taken at midnight holds none of the night's bookings, and restoring it would erase more.

diagram.aria: The fix replayed for 22 October. At 00:50:30 B starts term 2 and C votes for it, so B leads. Booking 112 for row 7 goes from B to C in term 2, and C answers that it is stored: 2 of 3, so it is confirmed. A valley phone sends booking 137 for row 7 to A, which answers waiting, because it holds 1 of 3. At 01:30 B's message with term 2 reaches A; A steps down and its 50 unconfirmed entries are replaced. Outcome: 0 confirmed bookings lost.

explain.caption: The fix, replayed for 22 October. B leads term 2 with C's vote and confirms booking 112 once two of three servers hold it. A, cut off, can store booking 137 but not confirm it. When the link returns, the higher term makes A step down, and only entries nobody was promised are replaced.

fix.title: The fix: confirm after a majority, and elect only up-to-date servers
fix.text: Move the booking record onto etcd, which runs Raft across A, B and C, instead of the home-made rule. A booking is confirmed, and Hivebook's email sent, only once two of the three servers have saved it. Every election starts a new term; a server votes only for a candidate whose log is at least as up to date as its own, and a leader that sees a higher term steps down. A cut-off server then confirms nothing, so a rejoin never has two yeses to choose between. Keep the row check where it was: the leader refuses a second booking for a booked row before adding the entry. Put the three servers on separate links, so one switch can't cut off the leader, and have Hivebook try another server when its own can't confirm.

limits: The side cut off from the majority confirms nothing. On 22 October the valley floor would have waited 40 minutes unless Hivebook sent its bookings to B or C instead.
Three servers survive one being lost, not two. With two down or cut off from each other, nothing can be confirmed; five servers survive two, at the cost of more copies per booking.
Raft keeps one record the same everywhere; it does not stop two members booking one row. The leader still has to check the row is free before it adds the entry.

head: What the cooperative does
Good
Bad
rows: Bookings never stop; no extra parts.
Most bookings from both sides are kept.
3 confirmed bookings still erased; trusts two clocks.
Still 20 erased; the hills wait 10 minutes for a leader.
40 minutes with no booking; a slow C pushes the last to 03:04.
Majority and up-to-date votes (Raft, via etcd)
0 erased; keeps working with one server out.
The cut-off side waits; one more program to run.

explain.seniorTake: A record copied across servers is only as safe as the rule that decides what counts as confirmed and who may lead. Home-made rules such as longest wins or newest wins pick a survivor after the damage, when both sides of a split have already said yes. Consensus prevents the second yes: confirm only what a majority holds, give every election a term, let a server vote only for a candidate at least as up to date as itself, and make any leader that sees a higher term step down. That is Raft, and Paxos before it. Use etcd or ZooKeeper rather than your own; tune the election timeout for speed, never for safety; and accept that a server cut off from the majority must stop confirming.

realWorld.title: Ongaro and Ousterhout, 2014: why Raft exists
realWorld.text: The paper opens: "Raft is a consensus algorithm for managing a replicated log." On the older family: "Unfortunately, Paxos is quite difficult to understand, in spite of numerous attempts to make it more approachable." Their test: "A user study with 43 students at two universities shows that Raft is significantly easier to understand than Paxos".

realWorld.title: Raft: committed means a majority
realWorld.text: "A log entry is committed once the leader that created the entry has replicated it on a majority of the servers". A held its 50 on one server of three, so under Raft none would have been committed or confirmed.

realWorld.title: Raft: terms find a stale leader
realWorld.text: "If a candidate or leader discovers that its term is out of date, it immediately reverts to follower state." And: "If a server receives a request with a stale term number, it rejects the request." That is A stepping down at 01:30.

realWorld.title: Raft: the vote that says no
realWorld.text: "The RequestVote RPC implements this restriction: the RPC includes information about the candidate’s log, and the voter denies its vote if its own log is more up-to-date than that of the candidate." How to compare: "If the logs have last entries with different terms, then the log with the later term is more up-to-date. If the logs end with the same term, then whichever log is longer is more up-to-date." An RPC is one server's request to another.

realWorld.title: etcd: Raft in practice
realWorld.text: etcd's own comparison page says a change "only needs to go through the raft protocol to commit." It describes what etcd is for: "These are systems that will never tolerate split-brain operation and are willing to sacrifice availability to achieve this end." On the alternative: "ZooKeeper solves the same problem as etcd: distributed system coordination and metadata storage." And: "The Kubernetes API server persists cluster state into etcd."

asked: How does Raft decide what is committed?
Why would a server refuse its vote?
When would you use etcd or ZooKeeper instead of your own?
interview.answer: Raft keeps one log on several servers with one leader. The leader adds each new entry to its log with its current term, sends it to the followers, and each follower saves it and answers. Once a majority holds the entry, it is committed, and only then does the system tell the client yes. A leader cut off from the majority can add entries but never commit one, so it never says yes. Leaders are chosen by election: a follower that hears nothing for its election timeout adds one to the term, votes for itself and asks the others. A server votes at most once per term, and refuses its vote to a candidate whose log is less up to date than its own, comparing the last entry's term first and then the log's length. That refusal is what keeps committed entries safe: any majority that elects a leader includes a server holding every committed entry, and that server only votes for a candidate that holds them too. A leader or candidate that sees a higher term steps down at once. I'd use etcd or ZooKeeper whenever several machines must agree on a small, important record: who leads, who holds a lock, which configuration is live. Getting consensus right is hard, Paxos especially, and the proven tools have years of testing behind them. I'd tell the story of a beekeepers' cooperative whose home-made rule, longest record wins, let a cut-off server confirm 50 bookings alone and then erase 20 that two servers had stored. With a majority to confirm and up-to-date votes, the cut-off server confirms nothing and nothing confirmed is lost.

terms.def: A group of beekeepers who share the work of booking hives into growers' orchards. Hedvig is its secretary.
One line of trees in an orchard. At the cooperative, one row takes 40 hives, booked by one member.
The shed where honey is spun out of the combs. The cooperative's server A sits there.
The strip of ground at the end of an orchard's rows, where vehicles turn.
The cooperative's booking app. Members book rows on their phones, and it emails a confirmation once a booking counts as confirmed.
A computer that answers requests over a network. The cooperative has three: A, B and C.
A numbered list of every booking, one entry after another, kept the same on every server. In Raft it is called the log.
One line in the record: one booking with its number, row, member and timestamp.
The one server that takes every booking, adds it to its record and copies it to the others. The others are followers.
A server that takes entries from the leader, saves them and answers. A follower that hears nothing for its election timeout starts an election.
A booking the system has promised to keep, and told the member so. In Raft an entry is committed once a majority of servers have saved it.
The servers choosing a new leader. At the cooperative, the longest record led; in Raft, a candidate needs votes from a majority.
How long a server waits without hearing from a leader before it starts an election. The cooperative's was 30 seconds.
Servers that can't reach each other for a while, each side still running. Also called a partition.
Servers reaching each other again after a split, when the rules decide which record survives.
The time on a server's clock when it stored an entry. Two servers' clocks never agree exactly.
Two confirmed bookings for the same row, made on two sides of a split. The sim calls it a clash.
A box that joins several cables so the computers on them can talk. A new one in the shed joined A's cable to the office.
A server that can't reach the others. A was cut off from B and C from 00:50 to 01:30, but could still reach members' phones.
More than half of the servers: two of three, three of five. Any two majorities of the same servers share at least one.
Holding everything that has been confirmed. Raft compares two logs by the term of their last entries first, then by length.
A numbered period with at most one leader. Every election starts a new term, one higher than the last.
A server asking to become leader. It adds one to the term, votes for itself and asks the others for their votes.
A server's yes to one candidate. In Raft each server gives at most one per term, only to a candidate at least as up to date as itself.
A leader or candidate going back to follower because it has seen a higher term than its own.
Several servers agreeing on one value or one record even when some fail or are cut off, like a group vote that never goes back on a result.
A consensus method built to be easy to understand: one leader per term, entries committed on a majority, votes only for up-to-date candidates.
The older consensus family, by Leslie Lamport: a value is chosen once a majority accepts the same numbered proposal. Proven safe and hard to follow.
An open-source program that keeps a small record on several servers using Raft. Kubernetes keeps its cluster state in it.
An open-source coordination service that keeps a small shared record on several servers, the other common choice beside etcd.
Open-source software that runs and restarts programs across a group of machines. It stores what it knows about them in etcd.
A group of machines working together as one service.
Short for remote procedure call: one server asking another to do something and waiting for the answer.
Two servers each acting as the only leader at once, as A and B did from 00:50:30 to 01:30.
A merge rule that keeps the entry with the later timestamp and drops the other, whatever was promised about it.
A saved copy kept so things can be put back after a loss. A nightly backup holds nothing made after it was taken.
Write it in the logbook before you do it. Never after. Write the record of a change, and save it to disk, before making the change.
Never trust the clock on the wall. One of the seven rules; Season 8 teaches it.
A booking never confirmed and gone from the final record, which the member's app sends once more after the link is back.
A setting in which C takes 2 minutes to store each entry, to show what waiting for every server costs.
The hands-on project Zones, regions and partitions, unlocked after s8e01, s8e04 and s8e06.
The hands-on project Three regions that must agree, unlocked after s8e01, s8e03, s8e04 and s8e10.
An international standard for running information security. Annex A 8.14 covers redundancy of information processing facilities.

atWork: Look for any place where several copies of a record choose a survivor with a home-made rule after they lose touch: "the longest log wins", "the newest timestamp wins", "the primary that comes back first keeps its data". It is a common pattern in hand-built failover scripts, in databases replicated by a script, and in job schedulers that keep their own state on two or three machines. For each, ask three things. When is a write confirmed to the caller: after one copy has saved it, or after a majority? If a server cut off from the others can still confirm, two sides of a split can both say yes, and some yes will be broken. Who may become leader: anyone whose record is longest or newest, or only a candidate at least as up to date as a majority of voters? And is there a term number, so a stale leader learns it is stale and steps down? If the answers are one copy, longest, and no term, move that state onto etcd, ZooKeeper or a database whose replication uses consensus, rather than fixing the rule by hand. Build Nights: this case unlocks L7, Zones, regions and partitions (with s8e01 and s8e06), and N6, Three regions that must agree (with s8e01, s8e03 and s8e10). Standards: if your company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, Annex A 8.14 (redundancy of information processing facilities) expects redundant systems to be tested so they work when needed; a failover rule that can erase confirmed records is a finding waiting to happen, so test a split and a rejoin from the first design, not at audit time.

recall.prompt: Your team keeps a job scheduler's state on three machines. After a network fault split one machine from the other two for ten minutes, both sides kept handing out jobs. When they reconnected, the side with more jobs overwrote the other, and jobs that two machines had accepted vanished. What went wrong, and what do you change?

keyIdeas.idea: The lone machine confirmed work on its own copy, so both sides of the split said yes
The longest-wins merge erased work that a majority had stored
Confirm only after a majority has stored it, and elect only up-to-date candidates with terms (Raft, via etcd or ZooKeeper)

recall.model: The lone machine kept confirming jobs on its own copy, one copy of three, while the other two elected a leader and confirmed jobs on two copies, so both sides of the split said yes. At the reconnect, the longest-wins rule picked the side with more entries and overwrote the jobs that two machines had stored. I'd move the state onto consensus, Raft through etcd or ZooKeeper: a job counts only after a majority has stored it, so the lone machine can't confirm anything, and a machine votes only for a candidate at least as up to date as itself, with a term on every election so a stale leader steps down.

recall.prompt: In the sim, with the cut on and everything else as built, which pair of settings loses no confirmed booking and still confirms the hills' 20 during the cut?
options: Confirm after one server, raft rules at rejoin
Confirm after two of three, longest record at rejoin
Confirm after two of three, raft rules at rejoin
Confirm after all three, longest record at rejoin
recall.why: Only a majority with raft erases nothing and keeps the hills booking: A confirms none of its 50, B confirms 20 in term 2, and at 01:30 A steps down. A majority with longest wins still erases the 20; raft with confirm after one erases A's 50; all three confirms nothing for 40 minutes.

recall.prompt: Under Raft, why would a server refuse its vote to a candidate?
options: The candidate's log is less up to date than the voter's own
The candidate's clock is behind the voter's clock
The candidate has fewer servers on its side of the network
The candidate asked before the voter's election timeout ran out
recall.why: A voter compares logs: the later last-entry term wins, and on the same term the longer log. If its own is more up to date, it says no. Because a leader needs a majority, and any majority includes a server holding every committed entry, no leader can be elected without them.

recall.prompt: In an interview you're asked: how does Raft decide what is committed?

keyIdeas.idea: The leader adds the entry with its term and copies it to the followers, which save it and answer
An entry is committed once a majority of servers have stored it, and only then is the client told yes
Votes go only to up-to-date candidates, so committed entries survive a change of leader

recall.model: The leader appends each new entry to its log with its current term and sends it to the followers; each follower saves it and answers. Once a majority of servers have stored the entry, it is committed, and only then is the client told yes. A leader cut off from the majority can't commit anything. Committed entries survive a change of leader because a server refuses its vote to any candidate whose log is less up to date than its own, comparing the last entry's term, then the length, and any majority that elects a new leader includes a server holding every committed entry.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 4 months later. etcd has held all spring; nothing confirmed has vanished. In January Hedvig added a fourth server, D, at the packing station, "for extra safety". On Tuesday 9 February 2027 a storm brought a tree down across the line between the farmyard and the packing station from 22:10 to 00:25. A and D sat on one side, B and C on the other. For 2 hours 15 minutes Hivebook confirmed no bookings at all, on a night we were moving hives to the clover.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Four servers are more than three, so why could nobody book, and what should Hedvig do?

keyIdeas.idea: With four servers a majority is three, and a two-and-two split leaves neither side with three
Use an odd number of servers: four survives no more failures than three
Place the servers so one broken line can't split them evenly, on separate paths

coldCase.model: With four servers a majority is three of four, and the fallen tree split them two and two: neither side had three, so neither could elect a leader or commit an entry, and Hivebook rightly confirmed nothing. Four servers survive one being lost, the same as three, and an even number adds a way to split evenly. Go back to three, or go to five servers so two can be lost, and place them on separate paths so one broken line can't cut the group in half.
